A node is two files: a manifest that declares its ports and knobs, and a script that runs it. Zip them and import from Flows, or push the folder to this app\'s plugin directory. No toolchain, no compile step, no new version of the app.

node.json declares the pack id, the node type, its inputs and outputs, its widgets, and which host ops it needs permission for.\n\nindex.js calls __nm.register(<pack>:<Type>, { run: fn }). Your run(ctx, inputs, widgets) returns whatever the last host op returned.

image.info width and height
image.resize image, width, height
image.crop image, x, y, width, height
image.new width, height, color
image.composite base, overlay, x, y, mask
image.blend a, b, alpha
image.grayscale, image.invert image
latent.blend two latents and a mask image

Inputs arrive as handles and host ops return handles. A 512 image crosses into your script as about 40 bytes of JSON rather than 780 KB, which is what makes the sandbox free. You never loop over pixels; you compose ops that do.

Give a number min and max and you get a slider. Give it options and you get a dropdown, or a row of chips when there are four or fewer. Add a hint and it shows under the control.\n\nYou choose the values; the app chooses the control. That is deliberate, so no pack invents a control language of its own.
What a node cannot do yet

There is no host op that runs a model, so a node cannot segment, detect or estimate anything. That is the next tier and it is not built.\n\nScripts run in a QuickJS sandbox and permissions are denied by default, so a pack cannot reach the network or your files. Nothing yet bounds how long one may run.
